overview: The modern Slovak Republic became independent on 1 January 1993 when Czechoslovakia divided peacefully. This is the republic that continues today, not the separate Slovak state of the Second World War. The map starts its modern label in 1994, after the actual founding.

periods.title: A separate republic
periods.summary: Slovakia established its own national institutions and diplomatic service after the Czechoslovak federation divided.

periods.title: European integration
periods.summary: Slovakia joined the European Union in 2004 and adopted the euro in 2009.

items.text: Slovakia’s first satellite, skCUBE, launched on 23 June 2017. The Slovak Organisation for Space Activities worked with universities and companies, and more than sixty volunteers contributed. A small spacecraft could bring together students, engineers and radio enthusiasts.

skCUBE suffered a problem shortly after launch, but ground stations in Slovakia continued receiving its transmissions. It operated for 569 days without a restart before stopping in January 2019. Engineering history includes learning from a mission that did not work exactly as planned.

The Danube dam dispute inherited by Slovakia began with a 1977 treaty between Hungary and Czechoslovakia. The project combined electricity generation, navigation and river engineering. Changing a river shared with a neighbor raised questions about water flows and the environment as well as machinery.

In April 1997, judges of the International Court of Justice visited the dam sites. It was the Court’s first site visit in its fifty-year history. Sometimes deciding an international legal case means putting down the paperwork and going to look at the river.

sections.title: Art, school and skills passed between generations

items.text: The Danubiana museum opened in September 2000 on a peninsula at the Čunovo reservoir, south of Bratislava. Dutch collector Gerard Meulensteen and Slovak gallery founder Vincent Polakovič helped create it. A waterside setting became a meeting place for Slovak and international contemporary art.

Danubiana’s collections include paintings by international artists, contemporary Slovak work and outdoor sculpture. Its history records a move into a nonprofit public institution with majority state participation in 2012. Caring for modern art involves collections, buildings and long-term public support.

Puppetry in Slovakia includes families who carve figures, make costumes, write stories and perform them. Children can meet the craft through workshops and performances, while experienced puppeteers teach newcomers. One small wooden character may require several different people’s skills.

The fujara is an unusually long wooden pipe with just three finger holes, associated with shepherds in central Slovakia. Makers often decorate their instruments individually. The older pastoral tradition continues through musicians and craftspeople, giving this very tall instrument a life beyond the sheep pasture.

Traveling tinkers once repaired damaged kitchen vessels using wire and tin. Today, the Považské Museum at Budatín presents both older work and contemporary wire designs. A practical skill for keeping a pot useful became a craft that could also make decorative objects.

The education ministry describes ten years of compulsory school attendance, lasting through the school year in which a pupil reaches sixteen. This is the modern educational system. Children’s learning has its own timetable, quite separate from the much older history of the region.

On 1 January 2009, Slovakia replaced the koruna with the euro. For the first sixteen days, people could pay using either currency. Shops and families had to learn new prices, with one euro officially equal to 30.1260 koruna.

Slovak, article 1 of the constitution: “Slovenská republika je zvrchovaný, demokratický a právny štát.” Translation: “The Slovak Republic is a sovereign, democratic state governed by law.” This wording is taken from Parliament’s official 2019 consolidated edition of the constitution originally adopted in 1992.

ending.text: The Slovak Republic continues as an independent state. Its modern beginning was the agreed division of Czechoslovakia in 1993, rather than a conquest or the disappearance of the communities that had lived together in the federation.
